title: What Is a Good IB Score? Grades and Goals Explained
summary: What is a good IB score? Understand IB grades, dated average scores, university requirements, and grade boundaries to set a realistic target for your next step.
body_markdown:
**A good IB score is generally around 32-35 out of 45, while 36-39 is very strong and 40 or above is excellent.** These are practical descriptions, not official IB categories. For university admission, a good score is one that meets your chosen course’s overall requirement, Higher Level grades, and subject prerequisites.


Imagine a student opening a report showing 34 points. At first, the number feels reassuring. Then a friend mentions 39, a parent asks whether 34 is enough for university, and the reassurance disappears.


The number has not changed. The comparison has.


Making sense of IB grades means giving that number the right context: how the diploma works, what your next step requires, and where improvement would make the biggest difference.


### What is a good IB score? A quick overview


Use this table as an informal guide, rather than an admissions rulebook.


Total score Practical interpretation


24-29 May meet the diploma points threshold, but all other passing conditions must also be satisfied


30-31 Close to the May 2025 global average; usefulness depends on your intended course


32-35 A good overall result, subject to your goals and subject grades


36-39 A very strong overall result, though selective courses may require particular HL grades


40-45 An excellent overall result, without guaranteeing university admission


Before judging a result, check three things:


- Is it a predicted score, a practice estimate, or a final result?
- Does it satisfy the relevant diploma and university requirements?
- Which individual subject grades sit behind the total?


A score becomes useful when it helps you make a decision.


### Understand what the score contains


The IB Diploma has a maximum of 45 points. Six subjects are graded from 1 to 7, contributing up to 42 points. Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay together contribute up to three additional points.


Creativity, Activity, Service does not add points, but completing its requirements is necessary for the diploma.


The minimum total is 24, but reaching 24 does not automatically mean passing. The IB also sets conditions covering subject grades, HL and SL totals, and the core. Check the[official IB diploma passing criteria](https://www.ibo.org/about-the-ib/what-it-means-to-be-an-ib-student/recognizing-student-achievement/about-assessment/dp-passing-criteria/) with your coordinator when interpreting a borderline result.


For our hypothetical student, 34 could represent six subject grades totalling 32 plus two core points. That breakdown matters because universities may specify subject grades separately from the overall total.


Parents wanting a clearer explanation can use RevisionDojo’s[guide to IB grade boundaries for parents](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-grade-boundaries-explained-parent-guide) to understand the distinction between marks, grades, and diploma points.


### Compare with a dated benchmark carefully


The IB reported a global average Diploma Programme score of **30.58 for the May 2025 session** , according to its[May 2025 results announcement](https://www.ibo.org/news/news-list/ib-students-worldwide-receive-their-results-2025/) .


That is a historical comparison, not a forecast for another session. A score of 34 sits above that particular average. It does not establish a percentile, predict an admissions decision, or describe how difficult another student’s circumstances were.


Averages answer a narrow question: how does this total compare with one examination cohort? They cannot tell you whether the result meets your own plans.


Students considering a nearby score may find RevisionDojo’s[guide to interpreting an IB score of 31](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/is-31-a-good-ib-score-student-and-university-admissions-guide) helpful for thinking through that distinction.


A student holding an IB results sheet looks up at a mountain of university prospectuses, where an admissions officer holds a sign reading Check your course.


### A good score must fit the course


Our student next opens a university course page. This is where the total starts to acquire meaning.


Suppose, purely as an illustration, a course asks for 36 overall with HL grades of 6, 6, 6. A student with 37 overall and HL grades of 7, 6, 5 would still miss the stated HL condition. A higher total does not necessarily compensate for a required subject grade.


Read each course’s current requirements for your intended entry year. Record the overall points, HL pattern, required subjects, accepted mathematics course where relevant, and any additional selection requirements. Check whether core points are included in the stated total.


Meeting published requirements also does not guarantee an offer. Selection processes and competition vary.


The useful question becomes specific: “Does my combination of grades meet this course’s conditions?” That is much more actionable than asking whether 34 is good in every context.


### How IB grade boundaries affect your result


IB grade boundaries translate assessed marks into grades. A boundary is the minimum mark needed for a particular grade in a specified assessment context.


There is no universal percentage that always earns a 7 across every IB subject and session. When converting marks, check the subject, level, examination session, and whether the boundary applies to an individual component or the overall subject result. Component weightings also matter.


Our student might see 68% on a school assessment and assume it means a particular final grade. That interpretation is only as reliable as the assessment, weighting, and boundaries used.


RevisionDojo’s explanation of[how IB grade boundaries are calculated](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-grade-boundaries-how-theyre-actually-calculated) provides useful background. Treat practice conversions as estimates rather than promises about final results.


### Turn the target into a practical study plan


Once our student understands the 34, the next task is choosing where to focus.


Start with a required subject that falls below a course condition. Then examine recurring errors: missing knowledge, weak application, incomplete explanations, or poor timing. These problems need different responses.


RevisionDojo brings the relevant resources together. Use Study Notes to repair a knowledge gap, Flashcards to practise recall, and the Questionbank to apply that knowledge. Its[guide to using an IB question bank effectively](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-question-bank-or-how-to-use-it-effectively) explains how to make practice more purposeful.


AI Chat can help unpack an explanation, while Grading tools offer feedback to review alongside mark schemes and teacher guidance. Mock Exams help you practise pacing; Predicted Papers provide additional practice without guaranteeing examination content. Read the[RevisionDojo Mock Exams guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/revisiondojo-mock-exams) before planning a timed session.


The Coursework Library and Tutors can support work that needs examples or individual guidance. Follow your school’s academic integrity requirements throughout.


A useful weekly goal is concrete: complete a focused question set, identify the recurring error, and retry it independently.


### Give the number a useful job


A good IB score should help you understand your options and choose your next action. For parents, that means discussing requirements and progress alongside the headline total. For students, it means setting targets that connect to real plans.


Our hypothetical student still has 34. Now, though, the number comes with a clearer explanation and a manageable next step.


For exact conversions using the relevant published boundaries, open RevisionDojo’s[Grade boundaries tool](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grade-calculator) . Match the subject, level, and session carefully, then use RevisionDojo’s study resources to work on the gap your results reveal.
